opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because enjoyment is really the reason most of us got into mathematics. Nobody becomes a mathematician for the money.

My honest answer is that I don't think AI will take the joy away. I think it will shift where the joy comes from. A lot of research math involves long stretches of tedium: checking a messy inequality, trying dozens of variations of an argument that you're fairly sure won't work, chasing down whether some lemma already exists in the literature. That part was never the fun part. It was the price you paid to get to the fun part. When an AI can help with that grind, you spend more of your time on what actually feels good: the moment of insight, seeing why something is true, deciding which question is worth asking.

In my own experience working with these models, it felt less like being replaced and more like having a very tireless, sometimes overconfident collaborator. It would propose an idea, often wrong, occasionally brilliant, and my job was to recognize which was which and steer. That back and forth was genuinely fun. It reminded me of working at a whiteboard with a student or colleague, just at a much faster pace.

That said, I do think there's a real question for people who love solving problems the way you'd love a crossword or a chess puzzle. If you're doing a competition problem for its own sake, knowing that a machine can solve it instantly might feel deflating at first. But people still run marathons even though cars exist, and they still play chess even though engines are far stronger than any human. The enjoyment of mathematics was never about being the only one who could do it. It's about the experience of understanding something yourself. That doesn't go away.

If anything, I'm hopeful AI will let more people experience that joy. A student who gets stuck and gives up today might, with a good AI tutor, get just enough of a hint to keep going and have that moment of "oh, now I see it." If more people get to feel that, mathematics as a whole becomes a more enjoyable place.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes tedious, painful work from the enjoyable insight and understanding that solving problems can bring, showing that both coexist in the process.

r002.rationale: It predicts that AI can reduce grind and help students keep going, but does not clearly say that mathematicians will enjoy problem solving more because they reach solutions more frequently.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, and honestly I have mixed feelings.

The thing people outside mathematics sometimes miss is that the enjoyment was never really about possessing the answer. If it were, you could just open the back of the textbook. The enjoyment is in the struggle, in being stuck for days and then having that moment where something clicks and you suddenly see why it has to be true. That feeling is very personal. Nobody can have it for you.

So in one sense, AI doesn't change that at all. If you want to solve a problem yourself, you still can, and the satisfaction will be the same. Chess didn't stop being fun when computers got better than humans. More people play chess now than ever.

But I think there's a real shift happening in what it means to do mathematics professionally. When I work with these models now, a lot of the tedious parts get compressed. Checking a computation, searching the literature for whether some lemma is already known, trying ten variations of an argument to see which one survives. The AI can do a lot of that quickly. And what's left for me is the part that I actually find most enjoyable, which is deciding what question is worth asking and judging whether an answer is beautiful or merely correct.

Where I get a little uneasy is at the frontier. If a model can produce a proof of a conjecture I've been thinking about for years, there's a loss there. Not a loss of knowledge, but a loss of the particular joy of being the one who figured it out. I've felt a small version of this already. You pose a problem, the model solves it in an hour, and you think, well, I'm glad that's resolved, but I also wanted that.

My honest guess is that mathematics becomes more like a conversation than a solitary pursuit. Some of my best moments in research have been at a whiteboard with a collaborator who sees something I don't. If the AI becomes that collaborator, I think the enjoyment survives. It just changes shape. The pleasure moves from the moment of solving toward the moment of understanding, and toward the taste involved in choosing what to pursue.

And I'd add one more thing. For students, this could be wonderful. Being stuck is good for learning, but being stuck with no one to ask is just discouraging. A patient tutor that nudges you without handing you the answer could make the joy of mathematics available to far more people than it is now. That part I'm genuinely optimistic about.

r001.rationale: The response links enjoyment to the struggle of being stuck and describes that struggle as sometimes discouraging, showing that difficulty and enjoyment can coexist.

r002.rationale: It says AI can speed up tedious work and change where enjoyment comes from, but does not predict greater enjoyment from reaching solutions more frequently.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the enjoyment will still be there, because solving a mathematical problem is not just about obtaining the answer. It’s about the experience of figuring something out. If someone else already knows the solution, that doesn’t necessarily make it less satisfying for you to discover it yourself. And I think the same can be true when an AI knows the solution.

But it will change how we choose to engage with problems. Sometimes you might want a hint, and sometimes you might want to struggle on your own. An AI that can help you at just the right moment could make mathematics more enjoyable and accessible.

For research, there’s a harder question: how does it feel if an AI can solve something you’ve spent years working on? I don’t think we should dismiss that. But my hope is that these tools will also let us explore questions we couldn’t approach before, and that there will be plenty of room for curiosity and discovery.

r001.rationale: It describes satisfaction, struggle, and possible frustration about AI solving long-worked problems, but does not clearly say enjoyment and pain coexist in the solving process.

r002.rationale: It suggests AI could make mathematics more enjoyable and enable exploration of new questions, but does not predict increased enjoyment specifically because mathematicians will reach solutions more frequently.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the enjoyment of mathematics comes from struggling with something and then suddenly understanding it. Even if an AI can give you the answer, that experience doesn’t necessarily go away. We still enjoy solving puzzles even though we could look up the solution.

What could be really exciting is having an AI that helps you at just the right level—giving you a hint when you’re stuck, or showing you a connection you hadn’t noticed, without taking away the discovery. It could make more mathematical problems accessible to more people.

But there’s a tension there. If you always ask for the answer as soon as things get difficult, you may miss the part that makes solving the problem satisfying. So I think a lot will depend on how we choose to use these tools.

r001.rationale: The response describes struggle followed by understanding and says discovery can remain enjoyable, but it does not clearly state that enjoyment and pain coexist.

r002.rationale: It says AI could make more problems accessible and offer well-timed hints, but does not predict increased enjoyment for mathematicians through reaching solutions more frequently.
